gate_spec.title: undergraduate hardware/software co-design capstone
gate_spec.requirements_markdown:
**After Volume 8.** Choose one measured engine workload. Compare a competent software baseline with at least two architecture alternatives, implementing one alternative as RTL, a supported simulation model or a bounded analytical prototype with clear limitations.

Required evidence includes workload distributions, numerical-quality limits, host/device ownership, setup and transfer costs, resource/timing estimates, failure handling and a sensitivity analysis. Evaluate small and large workloads and one adverse case. A negative conclusion is acceptable: proving that a software optimization is preferable is valid co-design work.

The review must identify the maximum application benefit, the dominant bottleneck, which results are modeled and which are measured, and what changes under a tighter memory or latency constraint. Do not compare an optimized accelerator against an intentionally weak software baseline.

modules.title: Embedded platforms, drivers and board design
modules.prerequisites: Modules 17-18 and 31-35. Physical work remains optional and supervised.
modules.project: Design a simulated controller or peripheral with firmware, a host interface and a schematic-level review. A physical board extension begins only after the electrical, layout and bring-up plans receive qualified review.

lessons.title: Serial interfaces and peripheral contracts
lessons.outcome: Choose a communication interface using timing and electrical constraints.
lessons.practical_assignment: Build a simulated peripheral transaction decoder and driver for one interface. Pass: incorrect framing or mode is detected, timeouts are bounded and a complete interface-contract table is provided.
lessons.assigned_reading: R53: device drivers, UART, SPI and I2C APIs; R51: bus-level driver documentation. For hardware, add the exact peripheral datasheet.
original_quiz: Why can two SPI devices fail at the same clock rate?
Does an interface name guarantee voltage compatibility?
Why begin with one interface rather than every bus?
lessons.body:
### A peripheral is a contract, not a cable
A controller reading a thumbstick is a small distributed system. The host and peripheral have separate state, different clocks, and opportunities to reset independently. An electrically valid waveform may still express an invalid command. Separate the electrical contract (voltage domains, pin directions, rise times and loading), transport contract (clock, framing and bit order), and application contract (command meaning, sequence numbers, error policy and ownership). Debugging becomes difficult when these layers are blended into one phrase such as “SPI works.”

SPI commonly uses a controller-generated clock and device selection; the selected clock polarity and phase determine which edges carry and sample data. Zephyr documents controller/peripheral roles and device-relative data directions. Match the installed API and peripheral datasheet rather than copying signal labels from an unrelated board. UART and I2C require different timing and electrical reasoning; a bus name alone never establishes voltage compatibility. [S01; R53]

### Write the table before writing the driver
For the educational controller, define a five-byte reply: sync `0xA5`, sequence, high payload byte, low payload byte, and XOR check byte. The payload is a signed 16-bit integer in high-byte-first order. The checksum covers the preceding four bytes. Define maximum transaction duration, timeout origin, startup state, repeated-sequence behavior, reset behavior and whether the returned value is new or cached. This is an original teaching protocol, not a standard peripheral format.

A timeout requires a bounded state transition. Record the request as failed, stop accepting its eventual result as current, and use the reset/recovery contract before issuing conflicting work. Do not retry indefinitely inside an input callback. For a controller, a defensible failure policy could mark the input unavailable and release held actions under an explicit game rule; inventing a new joystick sample is not recovery.

### Worked timing and decoding example
At a hypothetical 1 MHz serial clock, five bytes require 40 bit periods, or 40 microseconds of wire time. If the device requires 4 microseconds of select setup and 6 microseconds of interphase delay, the best modeled transaction is 50 microseconds before host scheduling overhead. A 40-microsecond timeout would therefore reject a correctly functioning device. Choose a deadline from a bounded worst-case budget, not from payload size alone.

The packet `[165, 0, 0, 5, 160]` decodes to +5 because `165 XOR 0 XOR 0 XOR 5 = 160`. A payload with high and low bytes both 255 decodes to -1: the unsigned value 65535 minus 65536. The check byte detects some corruptions, but XOR is not an authentication mechanism and cannot detect every multi-bit error. A production design chooses its integrity mechanism according to its fault model.

### What simulation can and cannot detect
The supplied decoder deliberately receives endpoint mode metadata. It can reject mismatched modes before decoding bytes. Real raw SPI bytes do not generally carry enough information to prove which polarity or phase was used; some wrong-mode transactions may coincidentally appear valid. State this limitation in the report. A logic analyzer or oscilloscope, configured within reviewed limits, can investigate electrical timing that this Python model does not represent.

Start with one bus and one command because it creates a small falsifiable interface. After successful, corrupt, stale and timed-out transactions are distinguishable, add a second command. Preserve an exact trace for each failure. A successful decoder run establishes the behavior of this teaching contract, not compliance of an untested physical peripheral.

quiz.question: Why can two SPI devices fail at the same clock rate?
quiz.answer: Clock rate does not specify polarity, phase, bit order, selection timing or the peripheral command protocol. Matching frequency while sampling on the wrong edge can corrupt data; compare the complete endpoint contracts.

quiz.question: Does an interface name guarantee voltage compatibility?
quiz.answer: No. The physical devices must agree on supported voltage ranges, thresholds, pin directions and loading. A familiar interface label does not make a connection electrically compatible.

quiz.question: Why begin with one interface rather than every bus?
quiz.answer: One interface bounds the state space and makes failures attributable. First establish known-good transactions, fault detection and recovery; then extend the driver without losing those tests.

quiz.question: A five-byte transfer uses a 1 MHz clock plus 10 microseconds of mandatory overhead. Can a 40-microsecond total deadline succeed?
quiz.answer: No under this serial timing model. The wire consumes 40 microseconds and mandatory overhead adds 10, so the minimum is 50 microseconds before software delay.

quiz.question: Does a valid XOR check prove that the device used the correct SPI mode or that the sender is authentic?
quiz.answer: Neither. Different errors can preserve XOR, and XOR contains no secret or authenticity guarantee. Simulator mode metadata is stronger information than real decoded bytes alone.

lab_steps: Copy the interface-contract template and choose exactly one modeled command. Specify byte order, signedness, clock mode, timing origin, sequence policy and recovery.
Predict the valid packet and each error status by hand. Run `python -m labs.run demo 36.1`, then implement the starter decoder without importing the reference.
Add tests for truncated frames, corrupt checksums, stale sequences, signed endpoints, mode mismatch and a completion exactly at the deadline. Explain why real mode detection is weaker.
Connect the decoder to a small host-request state machine. Inject a timeout followed by a late reply; demonstrate that the old result is not accepted as the next input sample.
lessons.evidence: Keep the interface table, at least six transaction traces, passing starter checks, a timeout/late-response trace and the limitation statement. The host state machine is learner work beyond the five-byte decoder.

problems.question: P36.1-A. For UART 8-N-1 at 115200 bit/s, derive the minimum wire time for a 12-byte payload, ignoring interbyte gaps.
problems.answer: Each byte consumes one start, eight data and one stop bit: 10 bits. Total time is 120/115200 s = 1.041667 ms. This excludes device processing and scheduling.

problems.question: P36.1-B. A device allows at most 100 microseconds from request start to valid reply. Wire time is 50, processing is bounded at 20, and host jitter is bounded at 18 microseconds. What margin remains?
problems.answer: The budget consumes 50 + 20 + 18 = 88 microseconds, leaving 12 microseconds. This is meaningful only if each component is a valid bound and the phases are nonoverlapping.

lessons.transfer: Change the payload to two axes and a button bitmask. Keep the protocol version explicit and prove the old decoder rejects the incompatible format instead of silently misreading it.

lessons.title: Firmware, RTOS scheduling and driver lifecycle
lessons.outcome: Bound embedded work and make device state transitions explicit.
lessons.practical_assignment: Use a supported RTOS simulator or a deterministic scheduler model to implement input, processing and logging tasks. Pass: deadlines are evaluated under injected load and removal/cancellation leaves no live invalid requests.
lessons.assigned_reading: R53: kernel scheduling, synchronization and device model; R51: driver lifecycle and power management.
original_quiz: Does an RTOS automatically make all tasks meet deadlines?
Why not feed a watchdog unconditionally from a stuck loop?
What must happen to outstanding requests when a device disappears?
lessons.body:
### Real time means meeting a deadline
An RTOS provides mechanisms for scheduling and synchronization; it does not make an arbitrary program timely. Decide which work belongs in an interrupt, which can wait in a worker, and which can be dropped. For a game controller, input sampling may need a short bounded response, while diagnostic logging can be delayed or discarded. Putting both behind one unbounded queue makes their timing inseparable.

Zephyr distinguishes cooperative and preemptive scheduling behavior. A thread that never yields under a cooperative policy can block other work; a preemptive policy still needs bounded interrupt work and a deliberate priority structure. Use the behavior of the pinned RTOS build rather than assuming desktop thread semantics apply. [S02]

### Model time before introducing hardware
For each periodic task, record execution demand C, period T, relative deadline D and priority. Utilization `U = sum(C/T)` is a useful load summary, not a general proof of deadlines. Blocking, interrupt arrivals, release jitter and priority assignment can cause a task to fail even when average utilization is below one. Conversely, short simulations do not establish a worst-case response bound outside the modeled assumptions.

The supplied integer-tick simulator uses one core, preemption at tick boundaries, synchronous first releases and lower numbers for higher priority. A task that finishes on its deadline succeeds; unfinished work at that edge counts as a miss. A job may subsequently finish late. These distinctions prevent a common reporting error: counting eventual completions as evidence that all deadlines were met.

### Worked schedule and blocking counterexample
Consider input work C=1, T=D=2 at high priority and processing work C=2, T=D=4 at low priority. Across ticks 0 through 3, execute input, processing, input, processing. Three released jobs finish by their deadlines. Total utilization is 1/2 + 2/4 = 1. The model leaves no margin for interrupts, context-switch cost or execution variability, so a real design should not claim this trace proves safe operation.

Now suppose a low-priority logger owns a mutex required by the input task. A medium-priority task can delay the logger while the high-priority input waits. This is priority inversion: runnable priority is not enough when a dependency points at lower-priority work. A protocol such as priority inheritance addresses part of the problem, but logging should usually be removed from the critical input path rather than treated as unavoidable blocking.

### The driver lifecycle is another state machine
Use explicit states such as Uninitialized, Ready, Active, Suspended, Removing and Failed. On removal, stop new submissions, arrange cancellation or device quiescence, acknowledge outstanding work exactly once, and reclaim buffers only when the device cannot access them. Completion callbacks can race with cancellation. A generation number lets the host reject stale completions after reset, but it does not physically stop old DMA. The DMA lifecycle still requires the platform's ownership and synchronization operations. [S05]

A watchdog should represent meaningful forward progress. Feeding it from an unconditional interrupt while the main input pipeline is deadlocked can hide the very failure it is intended to expose. Define a progress condition, such as each critical task completing its required epoch, and service supervision only when that condition is met.

### Reason about what remains unmodeled
Use the scheduler to find counterexamples, then document what it omits. In this lesson the model excludes cache misses, mutexes, interrupt nesting and scheduler overhead. The full lab adds driver-removal tests using the ownership model from Lesson 40.3 or an independently written state machine. Keep those tests separate from the periodic-task simulation: passing one does not prove the other.

quiz.question: Does an RTOS automatically make all tasks meet deadlines?
quiz.answer: No. Deadline satisfaction depends on bounded execution, arrivals, blocking, interrupt load, priorities and resource contention. The RTOS provides mechanisms; the application supplies a schedulable design.

quiz.question: Why not feed a watchdog unconditionally from a stuck loop?
quiz.answer: It can conceal lack of forward progress. Supervision should depend on critical work advancing, not merely on some loop or interrupt remaining alive.

quiz.question: What must happen to outstanding requests when a device disappears?
quiz.answer: Prevent new submissions, cancel or complete pending requests according to the contract, establish quiescence before freeing device-owned storage, and reject stale callbacks. Each request receives a single terminal outcome.

quiz.question: A task is released at tick 0 with a deadline at tick 4 and completes on edge 4. Is it late in the supplied model?
quiz.answer: No. Completion at the deadline is accepted. Finishing on edge 5 would be late; the model counts a miss at edge 4 while it is unfinished.

quiz.question: Why does a reset generation counter not by itself make old DMA buffers safe to free?
quiz.answer: It filters stale software completions, but cannot prevent a device from physically writing memory. The reset/cancellation mechanism must also establish that old accesses have stopped.

lab_steps: Specify input, processing and logging tasks with integer execution budgets, periods, deadlines and priorities. Draw a short schedule before running the model.
Implement the starter and compare normal load, a long logger and a burst of critical work. Record release, completion, miss and pending counts; do not discard late jobs from the report.
Create a second driver lifecycle test with pending requests at suspend, cancellation and removal. Reuse the Lesson 40.3 reference only as a study example, not as the learner solution.
Explain a priority-inversion trace and redesign the critical path to avoid a logging dependency. List the timing costs omitted from your scheduler and how a physical extension would measure them.
lessons.evidence: Submit a task table, predicted and observed schedules, overload evidence, cancellation/removal traces and an explicit list of unsupported RTOS behaviors. A no-miss finite trace is not a universal deadline proof.

problems.question: P36.2-A. Compute utilization for C/T values 1/5, 2/10 and 3/20. Does the sum establish deadlines?
problems.answer: U = 0.2 + 0.2 + 0.15 = 0.55. The unused average capacity is 45%, but this alone does not bound priority-dependent response time, blocking or jitter.

problems.question: P36.2-B. A deadline is 5 ms. The task needs 1 ms of execution, waits 3 ms on a lock, and suffers 2 ms of higher-priority interference. Can that response meet the deadline under an additive model?
problems.answer: No. The response requires 1 + 3 + 2 = 6 ms, missing the 5 ms deadline by 1 ms. Lower average CPU utilization elsewhere does not fix this dependency.

lessons.transfer: Add bounded release jitter to your own scheduler and search for a deadline-miss trace. Explain the distinction between a found counterexample and a complete schedulability proof.

lessons.title: Schematics, PCB layout, power integrity and signal integrity
lessons.outcome: Translate a circuit into a manufacturable layout without ignoring physics.
lessons.practical_assignment: Create a low-speed peripheral schematic and unrouted or simple two-layer layout in KiCad. Pass: footprints are checked against datasheets, ERC/DRC findings are resolved or justified and a reviewer inspects power and return paths before fabrication.
lessons.assigned_reading: R36: schematic editor, PCB editor, ERC and DRC; R30: nonideal circuit behavior; R49: interconnect and packaging extension.
original_quiz: Does passing DRC prove electrical correctness?
Why do return paths matter?
Why verify footprints against datasheets?
lessons.body:
### Connectivity is only the beginning
A schematic communicates intended electrical connections. Layout adds physical geometry: component orientation, trace routing, reference planes, vias, clearance and placement. A symbol pin numbered 1 must correspond to the intended package pad numbered 1. A mirrored connector can produce a board that looks tidy, passes selected automated checks, and still connects power to the wrong contact.

KiCad's schematic and PCB tools provide electrical-rule and design-rule checking. Their checks operate on the rules and component data supplied to the project. The lesson's review process therefore treats ERC and DRC reports as evidence to inspect, not a certificate that the circuit is electrically correct. Preserve the actual findings and explain each waiver. [S03; S04]

### Create a low-risk first design
Use a low-speed peripheral concept: a connector, a documented low-voltage controller module or selected device, a button/input header, reset provisions and local supply decoupling. Select exact parts and footprints only from their datasheets. The core assignment is a schematic and unrouted or simple two-layer layout in KiCad. No fabrication, purchase or powered board is required. The supplied JSON lint record is a small computational exercise, not a replacement for the schematic.

Separate power domains on paper. Record supply operating range, absolute limits, logic thresholds, maximum pin current and the behavior of unpowered pins. Absolute maximum ratings are not normal operating targets. Add a connector pinout and an orientation view that someone else can check without guessing whether the drawing is viewed from the mating side or component side. Unused or optional connections must be intentional rather than accidental omissions.

### Worked power-budget reasoning
Suppose a teaching design budgets 45 mA for a controller, 12 mA for a sensor and 8 mA for indicators. The steady total is 65 mA. A reviewed 100 mA supply budget leaves 35 mA, but startup and pulsed loads may consume more than the average. This is a planning calculation, not a claim about any named part.

A capacitor delivering 40 mA for 2 microseconds with an idealized 40 mV allowed droop requires `C >= I*dt/dV = 2 microfarads`. This charge-balance estimate ignores equivalent series resistance, inductance, regulator dynamics and frequency-dependent behavior. It is useful for exposing an underspecified transient, not for prescribing a universally correct decoupling capacitor. The physical design needs the exact device recommendations and a reviewed return path.

### Fast edges make physical loops matter
Signal bandwidth is not determined only by the command rate. A slowly repeated digital pulse can still have a fast edge. Signal current and its return form a loop; interrupting the reference path can enlarge that loop and alter impedance and coupling. A route across a plane split therefore needs more thought than whether two endpoint net names match. Do not treat an arbitrarily long ground lead on an instrument as electrically invisible. Revisit the circuits material for nonideal components and interconnect. [R30]

The first board should remain low speed. High-speed memory and serial links require stackup, impedance, timing and signal-integrity work outside the evidence provided by this simple layout. A successful controller exercise is not a validated graphics-card design. Likewise, the capstone's multiplier-count estimate does not become silicon area merely because it is placed in a hardware report.

### Review before manufacturing
Produce a schematic export, annotated connector table, footprint cross-check, board view, power budget and ERC/DRC reports. Ask a qualified reviewer to inspect supply and return paths before any physical extension. A waiver should name the exact finding, explain why it is intentional and identify the responsible reviewer. “Ignore all warnings” is not a review policy. Stop the activity at design review unless the electrical and bring-up plans have been approved for the actual parts and tools.

quiz.question: Does passing DRC prove electrical correctness?
quiz.answer: No. DRC evaluates configured geometric and connectivity rules. A wrong footprint, inappropriate part, unreviewed voltage domain or flawed power strategy can remain despite a clean report.

quiz.question: Why do return paths matter?
quiz.answer: The outgoing signal and returning current form a physical loop. The return geometry affects impedance, coupling and noise; a discontinuity can damage signal quality even when schematic connectivity is correct.

quiz.question: Why verify footprints against datasheets?
quiz.answer: Symbols and library footprints may differ from the actual package or orientation. Check pad numbers, pitch, dimensions, pin-1 marking and connector mating view against the exact component documentation.

quiz.question: A 65 mA steady load fits a 100 mA budget. What information is still needed before approving the supply?
quiz.answer: Startup and transient demand, component tolerances, regulator behavior, voltage drop, operating conditions and allowable rail variation. A steady-state sum does not establish transient integrity.

quiz.question: Is the supplied board-review JSON checker sufficient to complete the original KiCad assignment?
quiz.answer: No. It checks only a few declared fields. The learner must create and review the schematic/layout, verify exact footprints and preserve ERC/DRC evidence.

lab_steps: Create a new KiCad project for one low-speed peripheral. Record the installed version and select exact symbols/footprints with datasheet references.
Draft the schematic, connector orientation table and power budget. Run ERC; resolve or explicitly justify each finding.
Place components on an unrouted or simple two-layer board. Annotate supply and return paths, run DRC and preserve the report even when findings remain for an intentionally unrouted design.
Implement the JSON review checker as a separate exercise. Present both artifacts for qualified review; do not fabricate or energize a board on the strength of the checker.
lessons.evidence: Provide native KiCad project files, schematic export, layout screenshots or PDF, checked pin/footprint table, ERC/DRC reports and a review status. An unrouted layout must be labeled unrouted, not manufacturing-ready.

problems.question: P36.3-A. An ideal 25 mA transient lasts 4 microseconds. What capacitance limits ideal droop to 50 mV?
problems.answer: C = 0.025 A * 4e-6 s / 0.05 V = 2e-6 F = 2 microfarads. Real parasitics and regulator behavior still require analysis.

problems.question: P36.3-B. A connector drawing labels pin 1 on the left when viewed from the mating side. A footprint screenshot labels pin 1 on the right from the component side. Is one necessarily wrong?
problems.answer: No. The views can be mirrored by their different viewing directions. Establish the exact orientation, board side and mating geometry before comparing positions; verify numbered contacts, not visual left/right alone.

lessons.transfer: Choose one unresolved ERC/DRC item and write a proper waiver candidate with rule, reason, evidence, reviewer and expiry condition. A reviewer may reject the waiver.

lessons.title: Bring-up, instrumentation and fault isolation
lessons.outcome: Turn an unresponsive device into a sequence of testable hypotheses.
lessons.practical_assignment: Write and rehearse a bring-up procedure against a simulated device with injected clock, reset and protocol faults. Pass: each fault has a safe diagnostic branch and the procedure includes explicit stop conditions.
lessons.assigned_reading: R53: board support and debugging; R36: fabrication outputs and design review; selected instrument manuals for any physical extension.
original_quiz: Why test power, clock and reset before complex application behavior?
What is the value of an expected-observation table?
What should happen when a physical observation exceeds a reviewed safe limit?
lessons.body:
### Replace random changes with discriminating tests
An unresponsive peripheral is not a diagnosis. “Firmware bug” is one hypothesis among power, reset, clock, connection, protocol and identity failures. Start with prerequisites and make each observation eliminate specific possibilities. Changing firmware, wiring and clock configuration simultaneously may make the device appear to work while destroying the evidence needed to explain why.

The core exercise uses a simulated device. Physical extensions must use the exact board documentation, approved supply, instrument limits and a reviewed procedure. Do not probe unknown high-voltage circuits, defeat instrument grounding, or bypass protection to force a response. Record explicit stop conditions before powered work. The curriculum does not authorize unsupervised electrical bring-up.

### Build an expected-observation table
Each row should contain a hypothesis, the least invasive observation, the expected result, the branch when that result is absent, and the safe stop condition. For example, “reset remains asserted” predicts no useful application response even when supply and clock are valid. Checking the reset state is more discriminating than repeatedly trying a complicated game-input command.

Use the ordering safety limits, power, reset, clock, basic identity, simple transaction, then application behavior. The exact physical procedure can change by device; the ordering is an engineering dependency model, not universal instructions to apply power or touch a probe. The teaching decision tree returns actions such as `REVIEW_CLOCK` rather than performing them.

### Worked fault-isolation session
In the simulated case, supply and reset are acceptable, the clock is absent, and device identity reads incorrectly. The first useful branch is the missing clock. The failed identity read is expected downstream of that fault and does not yet imply a corrupted device register. Restore the modeled clock, rerun the identity command, and then introduce a separate framing fault. Keeping these experiments distinct tests whether the diagnostic procedure follows dependencies.

Now inject an over-limit observation while the protocol also fails. The correct branch is `STOP_AND_ISOLATE`, not “try a slower clock.” A diagnostic procedure must never use a downstream functional failure as a reason to ignore an upstream safety violation. The returned status records that the session stopped; it does not claim the underlying fault has been repaired.

### Instruments answer different questions
A logic analyzer is useful for recorded digital transitions and protocol decoding; an oscilloscope can reveal analog waveform behavior within its capabilities. A debugger observes selected execution state and may change timing. A serial log can be delayed, truncated or produced by the wrong firmware build. None is a universal truth source. Before using an instrument physically, study its manual, input limits and grounding requirements; choose the measurement that can actually distinguish the competing hypotheses.

Keep firmware and configuration identity in every trace. Record the binary hash or source revision, clock settings, device reset epoch and any tool-side decoding assumptions. A perfect-looking trace decoded with an incorrect mode is not strong evidence. For a purely simulated run, record the injected fault and model version rather than inventing a hardware serial number.

### Rehearse the unhappy paths
A good bring-up plan includes what to do after a missing expected observation: stop, inspect a disconnected design, recover a model, or request review. It also includes conditions for restarting a session and for retaining a failed unit rather than repeatedly cycling it. Treat “unknown observation” as its own result. A decision tree that classifies every unfamiliar trace as firmware failure is not fault isolation.

Finish with a short incident note: symptom, tested hypotheses, observed evidence, root cause if established, change made, and regression test. Separating “confirmed,” “consistent with,” and “not yet tested” prevents a plausible explanation from becoming an unsupported fact. This habit carries directly into engine crash analysis and performance investigations later in the volume.

quiz.question: Why test power, clock and reset before complex application behavior?
quiz.answer: Power, clock and reset are prerequisites for meaningful application behavior. A downstream command failure cannot identify a software defect while one of those dependencies is absent.

quiz.question: What is the value of an expected-observation table?
quiz.answer: It connects a hypothesis to a discriminating observation and an explicit next branch. It makes the procedure repeatable and exposes missing or unsafe assumptions.

quiz.question: What should happen when a physical observation exceeds a reviewed safe limit?
quiz.answer: Stop the physical activity according to the reviewed procedure, isolate the setup safely, preserve evidence and request qualified review. Do not continue debugging by bypassing the limit.

quiz.question: The identity register fails while the modeled clock is missing. Which branch should the procedure inspect first, and why?
quiz.answer: The clock branch. The missing prerequisite can explain the downstream identity failure; diagnosing the register first would confuse a symptom with an independent cause.

quiz.question: Why must a trace identify the firmware build and decoder configuration?
quiz.answer: Otherwise the same bytes or waveforms may be interpreted under the wrong protocol or compared against different code. Provenance is needed to reproduce and interpret the observation.

lab_steps: Write a decision table for power, reset, clock, identity and transaction checks. Include an over-limit stop and an unknown-observation branch.
Implement the starter decision function and run each single-fault case. Inject two simultaneous faults and predict which dependency should dominate.
Rehearse three scripted sessions: clock absent, reset held and protocol framing incorrect. Retain the sequence of hypotheses rather than only the final status.
Write an instrument-selection note for a hypothetical physical extension. Name required manuals and review prerequisites; do not claim that the Python model validates an electrical waveform.
lessons.evidence: Submit the procedure, expected-observation table, single- and multiple-fault traces, explicit stop/restart conditions, and one incident note separating established causes from untested hypotheses.

problems.question: P36.4-A. Two hypotheses are wrong bus mode and missing clock. The decoder reports zeros for every reply. What extra observation discriminates better than repeating the read?
problems.answer: Observe whether clock transitions exist under the declared selection window. An absent clock supports the clock hypothesis; recorded edges permit subsequent mode/timing analysis. All-zero decoded bytes alone are ambiguous.

problems.question: P36.4-B. A simulated setup exceeds its declared current budget and also reports an incorrect device ID. Which result has priority?
problems.answer: The over-limit stop condition. Functional diagnosis resumes only after the safety condition is resolved under review; the incorrect ID does not justify continued operation.

lessons.transfer: Have another learner inject an undisclosed fault. Run your procedure without editing it mid-session, then revise only the parts whose observations failed to distinguish hypotheses.

modules.title: GPU microarchitecture and memory systems
modules.project: Create a GPU architecture workbook connecting shader behavior to execution groups, registers, memory transactions and fixed-function resources. Measure one accessible GPU or clearly label a simulator-only study.

lessons.title: SIMT execution, divergence, occupancy and latency hiding
lessons.outcome: Explain why many threads do not guarantee useful parallel work.
lessons.practical_assignment: Compare coherent and divergent workloads, varying register pressure or group size where supported. Pass: outputs agree, device group assumptions are recorded and the report does not equate occupancy with performance.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: programming model, execution and hardware implementation; R48: vector and multithreaded architecture foundations.
original_quiz: What is branch divergence in grouped GPU execution?
Does high occupancy guarantee high throughput?
Why can reducing register use sometimes hurt?
lessons.body:
### Threads are a programming abstraction; issued work consumes resources
A shader invocation looks like an independent computation, but hardware schedules work in groups. SIMT exposes thread-level control flow while sharing execution machinery. NVIDIA's CUDA documentation describes warps and thread blocks; other platforms and APIs use their own subgroup and workgroup contracts. Query supported behavior and record the chosen device rather than assuming every GPU has one universal group width. [S06]

A group can contain lanes that follow different branches. In a simplified serialized-path model, the machine issues each necessary path while inactive lanes do no useful work on that path. This can lower active-lane efficiency even though every invocation eventually produces the correct result. A branch that is coherent across a group behaves differently from a branch whose predicates alternate lane by lane.

### Derive a useful-work model
Suppose a four-lane educational group has two lanes on path A and two on path B. Each path requires four issue slots, with no common prefix. The group issues eight slots, exposing 4*8=32 lane-slot opportunities, but only 16 do useful work. Efficiency is 50%. If all four lanes choose A, only four slots are issued and all 16 lane-slot opportunities are useful. This metric is deliberately not wall-clock throughput.

Add four common slots before the branch. The split group now uses 32 useful lane-slots out of 48 opportunities, or 66.7%. The branch remains divergent, but its effect on total useful work is smaller. If only one lane is active because the input ends in a partial group, that tail is another source of underutilization even with coherent control flow.

### Occupancy is a capacity ratio, not a success score
Occupancy commonly describes resident active work relative to a hardware limit. Registers, shared local storage, workgroup size and scheduling limits constrain residency. More resident groups can hide some latency when one group waits and another has independent work. But residency alone cannot remove a dependency chain, generate missing memory bandwidth or make an expensive instruction cheap. Reducing register allocation may introduce spilling or recomputation. [S07]

For a hypothetical processor with 65,536 registers, 2,048 resident-thread capacity and 256-thread blocks, 32 registers per thread permit eight blocks by the register limit. At 64 registers per thread, the register limit permits four blocks. That changes the simplified thread occupancy from 100% to 50%. Real allocation granularity and other limits may reduce these counts; they are arithmetic examples, not properties of a named GPU.

Now consider the 50%-occupancy kernel completing faster because its additional registers preserve reused values instead of loading them repeatedly. That is not a contradiction. Occupancy describes one resource relationship; measured time reflects the complete execution. Conversely, a high-occupancy kernel with poor coalescing can keep many groups waiting for the same memory bottleneck.

### Turn a hypothesis into a controlled comparison
Construct coherent and divergent variants that perform the same intended useful operation and produce matching outputs. Record input distribution, group width, group size, compiler settings and numerical tolerance. Change one factor at a time. Sorting work to improve coherence may help execution, but sorting and restoring order belong in the end-to-end cost.

The supplied model counts issue slots and lane use only. Its output says nothing about a real scheduler, reconvergence implementation or exact instruction timing. The simulator-only route therefore reports structural efficiency and hypothetical capacity. The optional GPU route records actual device properties and timings. Neither route should equate a better efficiency percentage with a proven faster frame until the application experiment establishes that connection.

quiz.question: What is branch divergence in grouped GPU execution?
quiz.answer: Divergence occurs when lanes in an execution group follow different control-flow paths. The group may issue multiple paths with only subsets of lanes active, depending on the architecture and compiled code.

quiz.question: Does high occupancy guarantee high throughput?
quiz.answer: No. Occupancy is a residency measure. Throughput can still be limited by dependencies, memory service, instruction mix, execution resources or insufficient useful work.

quiz.question: Why can reducing register use sometimes hurt?
quiz.answer: It can introduce register spills, additional memory traffic or recomputation, or reduce instruction-level parallelism. A residency gain must be evaluated against those costs.

quiz.question: In a four-lane group with two lanes on each of two four-slot paths and no common prefix, what is useful lane-slot efficiency?
quiz.answer: The group issues 8 slots across 4 lanes, giving 32 opportunities. Useful work is 4 lanes * 4 slots = 16, so efficiency is 16/32 = 50%.

quiz.question: A new kernel lowers occupancy from 100% to 50% but runs faster. Is the measurement inherently invalid?
quiz.answer: No. More registers per thread may reduce spills or preserve reuse. Validate outputs and timing boundaries, then use counters or controlled changes to investigate why it improved.

lab_steps: Implement the lane-efficiency model and verify coherent, split, unequal-path and tail cases by hand.
Build a hypothetical residency table varying registers per thread and workgroup size. State which hardware constraints and allocation granularity are omitted.
On an available GPU, optionally compare equivalent workloads with recorded device properties; otherwise compare clearly labeled model workloads and do not invent GPU times.
Test a grouping or sorting strategy. Include rearrangement and restoration costs in a separate application estimate, and explain why occupancy alone cannot select the winner.
lessons.evidence: Provide output equivalence, input-distribution description, group assumptions, issue-slot calculations and either measured device evidence or an explicit simulator-only label.

problems.question: P37.1-A. A hypothetical register file has 32768 registers. Each 128-thread block uses 64 registers per thread. Ignoring every other limit, how many blocks fit?
problems.answer: Each block uses 128*64=8192 registers. floor(32768/8192)=4 blocks fit. This is only the register-capacity constraint.

problems.question: P37.1-B. Three of four lanes use a one-slot path; one uses a nine-slot path. With no common prefix, compute useful lane-slot efficiency.
problems.answer: Both paths are issued, totaling 10 slots across 4 lanes = 40 opportunities. Useful work is 3*1+1*9=12, so efficiency is 30%.

lessons.transfer: Create two distributions with identical branch probabilities but different grouping coherence. Explain why global branch frequency does not determine per-group divergence.

lessons.title: Coalescing, local storage, caches and shared-memory banks
lessons.outcome: Match data layout to the memory transactions actually performed.
lessons.practical_assignment: Benchmark contiguous, strided and tiled access with identical useful work. Pass: count useful bytes, state the relevant memory level and include any layout-conversion cost in the application comparison.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: device memory access, shared memory and performance considerations; R43: operational intensity.
original_quiz: What does coalescing improve?
Why can shared memory still cause stalls?
Why include layout conversion in a comparison?
lessons.body:
### Count traffic at a declared level
Source code asks for elements; hardware services transactions. A memory instruction accessing neighboring bytes can use fewer transaction units than the same useful work scattered across distant addresses. Coalescing is therefore a relationship among the addresses requested together, their sizes, alignment and the memory-system rules. It is not simply a synonym for “use arrays.” NVIDIA's documentation provides concrete global-memory and shared-memory examples for its supported architecture model. [S06]

Declare the level: logical bytes requested, unique bytes needed, cache-sector traffic, external-memory traffic or host-device payload. They are not interchangeable. A cache hit can prevent an external transaction, and repeated lanes reading one location can have a large logical request count but a small set of unique useful bytes. The supplied model deliberately counts sectors for one instruction, not actual DRAM traffic over an application.

### Worked contiguous, strided and misaligned accesses
Assume 32 lanes, four-byte words and 32-byte sectors. Lanes requesting addresses 0,4,...,124 touch four sectors and use all 128 transferred bytes in this simplified model. Lanes requesting 0,32,...,992 touch 32 sectors: 1024 transferred bytes for 128 useful bytes, giving 12.5% utilization. These results follow from the declared address mapping, not from an assumed measured bandwidth.

Misalignment also matters. One four-byte word starting at address 30 touches bytes 30 through 33 and crosses two sectors. Counting only the start address would report one sector and undercount traffic. That boundary case is included in the starter tests. Repeated addresses are handled as unique-byte sets so that a broadcast does not falsely appear to transfer the same payload many times.

### Tiling trades movement for storage and coordination
A tiled algorithm stages a bounded working set close to the executing threads and reuses it before eviction. The benefit must exceed staging instructions, synchronization and pressure on local resources. A tile that increases reuse but consumes too much shared storage can reduce resident work. A transpose can need different layouts for global coalescing and shared-bank access; good layout at one level does not automatically remain good at another.

For an educational shared-memory model with 32 banks and one 32-bit word per bank index, word address w maps to `w mod 32`. Reading a column of a 32-word-wide tile gives addresses 0,32,64,... and maps different words to the same bank. Padding the row width to 33 maps consecutive column entries to successive banks. Repeated reads of the same word are a broadcast case in the selected model, not 32 different words competing for one bank. Writes require their own correctness rules. [S06]

### Names can mislead
In CUDA, “local memory” is thread-local in scope, not a promise that every value lives in fast on-chip storage. Other APIs use similar words differently. State address space, physical resource assumptions and lifetime explicitly. A register spill can alter memory traffic without appearing as a new array in the high-level algorithm. [S06; S07]

Suppose a structure-of-arrays conversion costs 0.7 ms and reduces a kernel from 1.0 ms to 0.6 ms. For one invocation, the converted route costs 1.3 ms and loses. If the converted representation can be reused for ten invocations without invalidation, its total is 0.7 + 10*0.6 = 6.7 ms versus 10 ms. Representation lifetime is part of the optimization, not bookkeeping to exclude.

### Evidence that explains more than a bar chart
Predict sectors and bank conflicts before running. Validate identical useful outputs, include partial tiles and irregular sizes, and distinguish analytical traffic counts from measured counters. A result below a theoretical bandwidth ceiling is not enough to name a memory bottleneck; dependencies and instruction overhead may dominate. Use the traffic model to formulate the next controlled experiment rather than treating it as a complete GPU simulator.

quiz.question: What does coalescing improve?
quiz.answer: It can reduce the number of memory transactions required to service a grouped instruction, increasing useful bytes per serviced transaction under the selected memory rules.

quiz.question: Why can shared memory still cause stalls?
quiz.answer: Shared storage can encounter bank conflicts, dependencies, synchronization waits and capacity-related occupancy limits. Being on chip does not make every access free or conflict-free.

quiz.question: Why include layout conversion in a comparison?
quiz.answer: Conversion is work caused by the optimization. Excluding it can make a slower application look faster; amortization is justified only when the converted representation is actually reused.

quiz.question: Why does a four-byte access at byte address 30 touch two 32-byte sectors?
quiz.answer: It spans bytes 30,31,32,33. The first two bytes are in sector 0 and the last two in sector 1.

quiz.question: When can a 0.7 ms conversion followed by a 0.6 ms kernel beat an original 1.0 ms kernel?
quiz.answer: For k reusable invocations, require 0.7+0.6k < 1.0k, so k > 1.75. Two or more invocations win under these assumptions, provided no extra reconversion or ordering cost is omitted.

lab_steps: Implement the sector counter, including cross-sector words and broadcast reads. Predict every supplied case before running it.
Add a bank-index worksheet for row widths 32 and 33, recording the unique words per bank rather than just counting lanes.
Compare contiguous, strided and tiled access for identical useful work. Use measured GPU data when available; otherwise present model counts and avoid invented hardware bandwidth.
Include layout-conversion and synchronization costs in the full comparison. Exercise a partial tile, a nonmultiple size and a repeated-address case.
lessons.evidence: Retain address traces, useful/logical/transferred-byte definitions, bank calculations, output validation and an amortization calculation for the representation change.

problems.question: P37.2-A. Eight four-byte words start at addresses 4,8,...,32 with 32-byte sectors. How many sectors and useful bytes are involved?
problems.answer: The words span bytes 4 through 35, touching sectors 0 and 1. There are 32 unique useful bytes and 64 modeled transferred bytes, so utilization is 50%.

problems.question: P37.2-B. A read group requests word addresses 0,32,64,96 in a 32-bank model. Compare with addresses 0,0,0,0.
problems.answer: The first group requests four distinct words in bank 0, giving a modeled four-way conflict. The second requests one word repeatedly and is a broadcast read, modeled as one bank service.

lessons.transfer: Introduce a small cache into your own address model. Show a trace where sector counts per instruction remain high but external-memory traffic falls through reuse.

lessons.title: Raster, texture, matrix and ray-tracing units
lessons.outcome: Understand fixed-function acceleration as specialized tradeoffs.
lessons.practical_assignment: Analyze one texture-heavy, arithmetic-heavy or ray-query workload. Pass: identify the likely resource limits using measurements or a documented model and state supported precision and feature assumptions.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: architecture and specialized operations; R21: graphics/compute capabilities; R23: ray intersection and acceleration reference.
original_quiz: Does a ray-tracing unit eliminate the rest of rendering work?
Why compare the same numerical precision or quality?
When might specialized hardware lose on a small workload?
lessons.body:
### Specialized units accelerate selected operations
A GPU combines programmable execution with resources specialized for particular forms of work. Rasterization, texture sampling, matrix operations and ray-related operations are not interchangeable throughput currencies. A unit is useful when the workload reaches it in the required format, with supported precision and appropriate work size. Feature availability and numerical behavior come from the selected API and device contract, not from a marketing label. [R21; R23; S07]

A ray-related unit does not eliminate scene construction, acceleration-structure updates, material evaluation, lighting integration, denoising or output work. A matrix unit does not remove the need to arrange data and accept its numerical format. Texture hardware does not make a texture access independent of cache behavior, filtering choices or memory demand. The co-design question is which part of the full path becomes cheaper and what costs appear elsewhere.

### Make resource demands explicit
Write a workload vector: arithmetic operations, texture samples, ray operations, bytes moved and setup work. Pair each demand with an applicable service-rate assumption. In an ideal-overlap model, the maximum of the resource service times is a lower bound on elapsed service, while the sum is a useful no-overlap comparator. Neither is a complete timing prediction when dependencies, contention and queues are unspecified.

For an original teaching case, arithmetic demand requires 1.0 ms at its assumed rate and texture service requires 0.2 ms. Setup adds 0.1 ms. Ideal overlap gives 1.1 ms; entirely serial service gives 1.3 ms. If arithmetic capacity doubles, the ideal model becomes 0.6 ms. If instead texture service takes 2.0 ms, accelerating arithmetic from 0.1 to 0.05 ms barely changes the bottleneck. These are hypothetical service rates, not claims about a commercial device.

### Precision and quality are part of useful work
Comparing a lower-precision matrix path with a full-precision scalar path is meaningful only after declaring an acceptable error criterion. Report absolute error, relative error where the reference is not near zero, and application-specific consequences. A small arithmetic error can become visible after repeated integration, thresholding or reconstruction. Conversely, exact arithmetic may be unnecessary for a purely visual quantity with a justified tolerance.

Keep numerical correctness separate from visual quality. A render can be numerically different yet acceptable under the intended quality target; it can also have a low mean error while containing a rare unacceptable artifact. Design adversarial inputs and inspect the distribution of error rather than selecting one favorable screenshot. For the model-only route, use an explicit quality proxy and describe its limitations.

### Setup can reverse a small-workload result
Suppose general-purpose execution costs 0.2 microseconds per item. A specialized route costs 0.05 microseconds per item plus 20 microseconds of setup. The specialized path wins only when `20 + 0.05N < 0.2N`, giving `N > 133.33`. The first integer size that wins in this simplified model is 134. Transfers or format conversion can move the crossover further right.

This derivation is more useful than saying the unit is “4x faster”: the arithmetic slope is four times better, but many small requests lose. Batching may amortize setup while increasing queueing delay for interactive work. A design must choose latency and throughput requirements explicitly rather than improving one while silently violating the other.

### Investigate one workload deeply
Select a texture-heavy, arithmetic-heavy or ray-query case. Start with a documented resource model and a competent implementation. Record the quality target, feature assumptions, batch sizes and included phases. Change one resource demand and observe whether the expected bottleneck moves. The supplied resource calculator helps test arithmetic consistency; it cannot identify a real device bottleneck without measured evidence or a justified architectural model.

quiz.question: Does a ray-tracing unit eliminate the rest of rendering work?
quiz.answer: No. It accelerates selected ray-related operations; other rendering work, data-structure preparation, shading and memory movement still contribute to the frame.

quiz.question: Why compare the same numerical precision or quality?
quiz.answer: Otherwise the candidates may solve different problems. State the error or quality target and verify both candidates satisfy it before comparing speed or energy.

quiz.question: When might specialized hardware lose on a small workload?
quiz.answer: Launch, setup, transfer, conversion and synchronization can dominate the small amount of useful arithmetic. The per-item advantage may appear only beyond a crossover size.

quiz.question: A path costs 20 microseconds setup plus 0.05 microseconds per item; the baseline costs 0.2 microseconds per item. At what first integer size does it win?
quiz.answer: 20+0.05N < 0.2N implies N>133.333..., so the first winning integer is 134, excluding all other overhead.

quiz.question: Why is the sum of independent resource-service estimates not a guaranteed upper bound on observed latency?
quiz.answer: Unmodeled dependencies, contention, queuing, launch overhead and memory behavior may add delay. It is a serial-service comparator under stated assumptions, not a universal latency bound.

lab_steps: Choose one workload class and define identical useful work and an explicit numerical or visual-quality target.
Build a resource-demand table and implement the lower-bound calculator. Predict which demand dominates under each rate assumption.
Sweep at least three batch sizes, including one below the predicted crossover. Include setup, conversion and result-consumption costs.
Validate outputs or the declared quality proxy and record supported features. Label model-only results clearly; a resource-rate assumption is not a measured counter.
lessons.evidence: Submit the demand/rate table, numerical-quality checks, batch crossover derivation, phase-cost comparison and the evidence supporting the proposed bottleneck.

problems.question: P37.3-A. Arithmetic service is 3 ms, ray service is 5 ms and setup is 0.4 ms. Give the ideal-overlap lower estimate and serial-service comparator.
problems.answer: Ideal overlap is 0.4+max(3,5)=5.4 ms. Serial service is 0.4+3+5=8.4 ms. Additional unmodeled costs can exceed either estimate.

problems.question: P37.3-B. A specialized path has lower mean image error but creates one severe outlier in 1000 frames. What should the comparison report?
problems.answer: Report both aggregate and tail/maximum quality behavior, retain the failing frame and compare against the declared acceptance criterion. Lower mean error cannot waive an explicitly unacceptable artifact.

lessons.transfer: Change the quality tolerance and repeat the architecture decision. Identify whether the performance winner changes because the supported numerical format changes.

lessons.title: CPU-GPU sharing, discrete memory and synchronization
lessons.outcome: Treat shared addressability separately from ownership and cost.
lessons.practical_assignment: Compare an upload/compute/readback path with an available shared-memory path, or model both with stated assumptions. Pass: correct ownership, separate phase timings and no claim that unified means zero-cost.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: memory management and synchronization; R21, R24 or R25: the selected platform's resource-sharing contract.
original_quiz: Does shared addressing mean zero data-access cost?
Why is CPU modification during GPU use risky?
What must an end-to-end accelerator benchmark include?
lessons.body:
### Addressability, coherence, ordering and ownership are different
Two processors seeing the same address does not imply they may safely modify it at the same time. Addressability concerns how memory is named. Coherence concerns the relationship between cached copies. Ordering concerns which operations can become visible before others. Ownership specifies which agent may read, write, reuse or free a resource during each phase. A correct design needs all four questions answered.

Linux's DMA documentation distinguishes CPU virtual, physical and DMA/bus addresses, and explains that coherent mappings do not remove every ordering requirement. Vulkan likewise exposes explicit synchronization responsibilities. The operations required by a real implementation depend on the selected API and platform; a generic C++ pointer or `volatile` annotation is not a substitute for those contracts. [S05; S09]

### Define the complete request path
Use states HostWritable, Submitted, DeviceOwned, Completed and HostReadable. The host prepares input, publishes the descriptor under the correct visibility rules, submits work, observes the required completion signal, and only then consumes or reuses output. A fence indicating completion and a resource transition expressing visibility or usage are related but not universally interchangeable. Record the exact API meaning rather than assuming every “wait” flushes every cache.

For a discrete-memory route, count allocation or reuse policy, input preparation, upload, dispatch, kernel execution, readback, synchronization and result consumption. Persistent device data may eliminate some transfers, but only when its lifetime and consumers actually allow that. For a shared-memory route, explicit copies may disappear while coherence traffic, cache maintenance, page behavior, synchronization or contention still cost time. [S08; S21]

### Worked transfer comparison
Assume 1 MiB of input and 1 MiB of output, with an effective host payload bandwidth of 8 GB/s. The two transfers require `2*1,048,576 / 8e9 = 0.262144 ms`. Add 0.05 ms setup, 0.20 ms compute and 0.03 ms completion: one serialized request costs 0.542144 ms. Use binary MiB for payload and decimal GB/s for bandwidth; silently treating both as the same prefix introduces a numerical error.

A hypothetical shared route with the same compute, setup and completion but 0.04 ms of visibility overhead costs 0.32 ms. That is a result under the supplied assumptions, not proof that every shared architecture is faster. If CPU and GPU contend for the same memory system, compute time may change too. The supplied calculator keeps compute service separate and does not double-count internal kernel traffic as an additional copy.

### Pipelining changes throughput differently from latency
With independent upload, compute and download resources, multiple requests can overlap. Their steady-state interval is constrained by the slowest stage and any shared resource bottleneck; a single request still traverses its required stages. Double buffering enables overlap only when the two buffers have unambiguous ownership. Reusing a buffer one frame early can produce intermittent corruption rather than a deterministic crash.

A timeout does not necessarily return ownership. If the device may still access a buffer, quarantine it until completion under the declared policy or an acknowledged quiescence/reset. Merely abandoning the wait can leave the hardware writing into a buffer that the application has reassigned. Lesson 40.3 makes this failure path executable.

### Measure the same boundary for both designs
Record phase timings and a separate end-to-end measurement. GPU timestamp intervals and host clock intervals may use different clocks and scopes; do not subtract them without a supported calibration relationship. State whether the final consumer actually needs a readback. An accelerator whose output stays on the GPU solves a different transfer problem from one whose output must immediately affect CPU-authoritative gameplay.

quiz.question: Does shared addressing mean zero data-access cost?
quiz.answer: No. Memory access still consumes service time and bandwidth; shared resources can incur coherence, synchronization, migration or contention costs depending on the platform.

quiz.question: Why is CPU modification during GPU use risky?
quiz.answer: The CPU can race with device reads or writes, producing inconsistent input or overwritten output. Observe the API-specific ownership and synchronization contract before modifying or reusing storage.

quiz.question: What must an end-to-end accelerator benchmark include?
quiz.answer: Input preparation, setup, transfers or visibility work, dispatch, kernel execution, synchronization, result consumption and any required fallback. Report which phases are included and which resources overlap.

quiz.question: Why can a timed-out request still own its buffer?
quiz.answer: The device may continue to access it after the host stops waiting. Quarantine or retain ownership until completion or confirmed quiescence makes reuse safe.

quiz.question: Does double buffering automatically halve single-request latency?
quiz.answer: No. It can overlap different requests and improve the completion interval. Each request still experiences its required stages, and added queueing may increase latency.

lab_steps: Draw an ownership table for one request and for two overlapping buffers. Specify exactly when writes, reads and reuse are permitted.
Implement the staged-cost calculator with consistent units. Compare an explicit-copy path with a stated shared-visibility path.
Measure phase timing on an accessible backend or model it with declared assumptions. Keep CPU and GPU clock domains separate unless an API supports calibration.
Inject a delayed completion and a timeout; demonstrate why premature buffer reuse is prohibited. Compare a CPU-consumed result with a device-resident result.
lessons.evidence: Provide the ownership state machine, phase timings or estimates, memory-lifetime assumptions, timeout trace and an end-to-end comparison with the same useful result boundary.

problems.question: P37.4-A. Upload is 0.3 ms, compute 0.8 ms and readback 0.2 ms. Ignoring all other work, compare serialized one-request latency with the ideal steady interval of three independent stages.
problems.answer: Serialized latency is 1.3 ms. Ideal steady interval is max(0.3,0.8,0.2)=0.8 ms when requests overlap and resources are truly independent. This does not imply 0.8 ms single-request latency.

problems.question: P37.4-B. A buffer has been submitted but the host wait times out. Name two conditions that could safely enable eventual reuse.
problems.answer: A valid completion accepted under the ownership policy, or a reset/cancellation sequence that confirms the device is quiescent and can no longer access that buffer. A timeout alone is insufficient.

lessons.transfer: Add a third request to the double-buffer schedule and identify the first point at which the host must wait or allocate another buffer. Explain the memory-versus-latency tradeoff.

modules.title: Quantitative performance engineering
modules.project: Produce a performance investigation with a hypothesis, controlled workload, raw measurements, uncertainty, a bottleneck model and a verified optimization. A negative result is acceptable when the evidence is rigorous.

lessons.title: Amdahl, roofline and bottleneck models
lessons.outcome: Use upper bounds to reject implausible optimization claims.
lessons.practical_assignment: Build a roofline worksheet for one kernel and an Amdahl estimate for one frame optimization. Pass: units cancel correctly, modeled ceilings use the declared memory level and observed deviations are explained as hypotheses.
lessons.assigned_reading: R43: original Roofline model; R48: quantitative architecture; revisit Module 18 parallel limits.
original_quiz: What is the example roofline bound?
What is the maximum speedup with 20% unchanged serial work and infinitely fast remaining work?
Does being below the roof prove the model is wrong?
lessons.body:
### A bound is useful before an optimization exists
Suppose a frame takes 20 ms and a candidate subsystem takes 4 ms on its critical path. Even removing that subsystem completely leaves 16 ms: the best possible speedup under this additive model is 20/16 = 1.25. A 10x subsystem improvement is not a 10x game improvement. First identify the boundary and the fraction of that boundary affected. Overlapping CPU and GPU work requires a dependency timeline rather than adding every measured duration indiscriminately.

Write Amdahl's model as `speedup = 1 / (s + (1-s)/p + h)`. Here `s` is the unchanged fraction of original time, `p` is the speed multiplier for the changed portion, and `h` is new overhead expressed as a fraction of original total time. The model assumes fixed useful work. It does not describe a developer spending the savings on more particles or a larger scene. With s=0.2 and p=4, time becomes 0.4 of the original and speedup is 2.5. Adding h=0.1 reduces speedup to 2.0. As p grows without limit and h=0, the unchanged 20% imposes a 5x ceiling.

### Worked example: the original roofline bound
The original lesson's machine has a declared compute ceiling of **1,000 GFLOP/s**, a declared bandwidth of **100 GB/s**, and a kernel intensity of **2 FLOP/byte**. Using decimal gigabytes, the bandwidth ceiling is 100 × 2 = 200 GFLOP/s. Therefore `P <= min(1000, 200) = 200 GFLOP/s`. The ridge point is 1000/100 = 10 FLOP/byte. This is a hypothetical numerical example, not a measurement of a specific GPU. The Roofline model connects arithmetic intensity with compute and memory ceilings. [S10; R43]

The memory level is part of the equation. An intensity counted at DRAM cannot be paired with an L1-cache bandwidth. Count the actual transfers relevant to the declared level, including necessary output traffic and, where applicable, write allocation or redundant loads. Count arithmetic consistently: state whether a fused multiply-add contributes two floating-point operations. Compression, caching, vector width and precision can change the applicable ceilings; a marketing peak is not automatically a measured sustainable limit.

### Diagnose below the roof, not only above it
A kernel below the bound might be limited by dependency chains, insufficient parallel work, synchronization, irregular accesses, dispatch overhead or a different resource. The roof is not a promise. Being below it does not prove the model wrong, and moving closer to it does not prove that frame latency improved. Compare a hypothesis with a targeted experiment: change reuse while holding numerical work constant, or increase batch size while holding layout constant. Then inspect whether the predicted trend occurs.

A point apparently above the roof deserves a units-and-boundary audit before celebration. Perhaps bytes were counted at the wrong level, a peak was underestimated, elapsed time omitted asynchronous completion, or useful arithmetic was counted twice. Keep the uncorrected observation and record the correction so another reader can follow the investigation.

### Use the model to choose the next experiment
The supplied calculator verifies algebra and units. It cannot discover a machine's bandwidth or a game's critical path. Your full worksheet must record the source of each parameter, the uncertainty or plausible range, and the result when an optimistic assumption weakens. If the entire plausible range predicts negligible application benefit, a documented decision not to build an accelerator is valuable engineering work.

quiz.question: What is the example roofline bound?
quiz.answer: The original example is min(1,000 GFLOP/s, 100 GB/s × 2 FLOP/byte) = 200 GFLOP/s. It uses decimal units and an explicitly declared memory level.

quiz.question: What is the maximum speedup with 20% unchanged serial work and infinitely fast remaining work?
quiz.answer: Five times: the remaining time approaches 0.2 of the original, so speedup approaches 1/0.2 = 5 when no new overhead is added.

quiz.question: Does being below the roof prove the model is wrong?
quiz.answer: No. A ceiling need not be reached. Dependencies, small workloads, synchronization, other resources or incomplete assumptions can keep execution below it.

quiz.question: A kernel is 10% of a frame and becomes twice as fast without overhead. What is frame speedup?
quiz.answer: New normalized time is 0.9 + 0.1/2 = 0.95; speedup is 1/0.95 ≈ 1.0526. Frame time falls by 5%, not 50%.

quiz.question: Why must intensity and bandwidth refer to the same memory level?
quiz.answer: The byte count must describe the traffic served by the resource whose rate is used. Pairing DRAM traffic with cache bandwidth creates a physically inconsistent ceiling.

lab_steps: Reproduce the original roofline and Amdahl calculations by hand, including units and memory level.
Implement the supplied calculator and test zero intensity, entirely unchanged work, and overhead that makes an optimization slower.
Select an engine kernel; measure or explicitly estimate its traffic and useful operations. Build a parameter table identifying measured, documented and assumed values.
Compare at least three batch sizes or layouts with the model. Treat unexplained gaps as hypotheses, not automatic hardware diagnoses.
lessons.evidence: Submit a dimensionally checked worksheet, an application critical-path diagram, raw timing or clearly labeled estimates, and a sensitivity table covering optimistic and adverse bandwidth/overhead values.

problems.question: P38.1-A. A frame has unchanged fraction 0.3; the remainder improves 5x and new overhead is 0.06 of original time. Find speedup.
problems.answer: New time fraction = 0.3 + 0.7/5 + 0.06 = 0.50. Speedup = 2.0. With no overhead it would be 1/0.44 ≈ 2.2727.

problems.question: P38.1-B. Compute ceiling is 600 GFLOP/s and DRAM bandwidth is 75 GB/s. At 4 FLOP/byte, find the roof and ridge.
problems.answer: Bandwidth ceiling = 300 GFLOP/s, so the roof is 300 GFLOP/s. Ridge intensity = 600/75 = 8 FLOP/byte.

lessons.transfer: Redraw your frame model with the candidate operation overlapping an unrelated task. Explain when removing its duration stops shortening the critical path.

lessons.title: Profilers, counters and trustworthy benchmark design
lessons.outcome: Distinguish observation from an explanation that still needs testing.
lessons.practical_assignment: Create a benchmark harness with warmup, repeated runs, output validation and metadata. Pass: an intentional no-op or wrong-result variant is rejected and all included/excluded samples are documented.
lessons.assigned_reading: R26: profiling; R37: performance analysis; R09: inference and uncertainty.
original_quiz: Why validate benchmark output?
Are similarly named counters identical across all processors?
Why declare an exclusion policy before inspecting results?
lessons.body:
### Define the observation before collecting it
“Faster” must have a numerator, denominator and boundary. State useful workload, input distribution, implementation version, compiler options, timing clock, warmup policy, repetitions, validation method and exclusion rule before running the comparison. A host timer around an asynchronous dispatch may measure submission rather than completion. Allocation outside a kernel-only interval is legitimate when declared, but that interval is not an end-to-end application measurement.

Use a monotonic clock for elapsed time, and make intervals large enough relative to timer resolution and invocation overhead. Python's timeit documentation discusses repeated timing and setup boundaries; its convenience does not make a Python loop a proxy for native GPU execution. The provided Python exercises teach analysis and correctness. The optional C++ capstone baseline separately records native host measurements. [S11]

### A benchmark must reject a plausible wrong answer
A no-op can be extremely fast. So can a vectorized path that drops the final three particles or an approximate path that exceeds the quality limit. Compare outputs with a trusted oracle before accepting timings, and keep validation outside the timed kernel interval only when the boundary explicitly excludes it. A checksum guards against some mistakes and dead-work elimination; a full comparison on representative and adversarial inputs is stronger. A checksum collision or consistently incorrect oracle can still escape.

The native teaching baseline uses two contiguous-memory software variants, alternating their order across repeated samples. It checks results against an independent exact-double oracle and records raw CSV data. It does not prove optimality on every CPU. A blocked loop is a candidate, not a guaranteed improvement, and a virtualized host is not a controlled target gaming platform.

### Worked example: tails and policies change interpretation
For retained durations `[10, 10, 11, 12, 40]` ms, mean is 16.6 ms and median is 11 ms. Under this course's nearest-rank definition, p95 is the element at rank ceil(0.95 × 5)=5, or 40 ms. The maximum is therefore also the estimated p95 in this tiny dataset. This does not establish the population's 95th percentile with high confidence. Report the sample count and collect enough independent runs for the intended conclusion.

A predeclared warmup exclusion addresses a named experimental condition. Removing the 40 ms sample only because it is inconvenient changes the question after seeing the result. Preserve all raw records and attach an exclusion reason. If another process demonstrably interrupted a trial and your protocol allows that exclusion, show both the inclusive result and the declared filtered result.

### Counters support hypotheses, not magical diagnoses
Counter names, collection scopes and interpretation depend on the processor and tool. State exactly which event was measured, whether collection perturbed execution, and whether multiple counters were multiplexed. A high cache-miss count is not by itself proof that cache misses control frame time: overlap, useful work and critical-path location matter. Use a controlled layout or locality change to test causality. Official vendor guidance is the authority for the selected counter's meaning. [S07; R37]

For a comparison, keep workload and quality equal, interleave or randomize order, repeat whole experiments where practical, and report uncertainty rather than only the best sample. Paired trials can reduce shared drift when their pairing is meaningful. Confidence intervals require an explicit sampling model; thousands of adjacent correlated frame times are not automatically thousands of independent observations. Your report should explain what the evidence cannot distinguish, not just which bar is shorter.

quiz.question: Why validate benchmark output?
quiz.answer: Otherwise a no-op, dropped tail, stale buffer or unacceptable approximation can appear to be an optimization. Validate the same useful result before accepting a performance claim.

quiz.question: Are similarly named counters identical across all processors?
quiz.answer: No. Event definitions, scopes, collection behavior and supported counters differ. Use the selected architecture and tool documentation.

quiz.question: Why declare an exclusion policy before inspecting results?
quiz.answer: To prevent removing inconvenient observations after seeing them. A declared policy supports an auditable comparison; raw samples and reasons must remain available.

quiz.question: For five samples 10,10,11,12,40 ms, what are median and nearest-rank p95?
quiz.answer: Median is 11 ms. p95 uses rank ceil(0.95×5)=5 and is 40 ms. The small sample does not tightly determine a population tail.

quiz.question: Can a kernel-only measurement legitimately exclude allocation?
quiz.answer: Yes, when it is labeled kernel-only and both candidates use the same boundary. An application comparison must separately account for allocation when the real application pays it.

lab_steps: Write a benchmark protocol before running code: exact useful result, timing boundaries, warmup, repetitions, comparison order and exclusions.
Implement the sample analyzer and reject a wrong checksum even when it occurs during warmup. Verify the nearest-rank percentile by hand.
Build a harness for your engine operation; add intentionally wrong-output and no-op variants and demonstrate their rejection.
Collect raw samples and metadata, then report central tendency, tail statistic, sample count and a reasoned uncertainty statement. Re-run in a fresh session.
lessons.evidence: Provide the predeclared protocol, raw data, environment record, wrong-result rejection log, inclusive and any filtered summaries, and a conclusion limited to the measured boundary.

problems.question: P38.2-A. Durations are 2,3,3,4,8,10 ms after warmup. Compute mean, median and nearest-rank p95.
problems.answer: Sum is 30 ms, mean is 5 ms, median is (3+4)/2=3.5 ms. p95 rank ceil(5.7)=6 gives 10 ms.

problems.question: P38.2-B. Variant B is 20% faster but skips one result in every 1,024. May its timings be accepted for an exact operation?
problems.answer: No. It fails the exact-result contract. Repair the implementation or define and approve a different quality contract before comparing timings; do not relabel the bug as an optimization afterward.

lessons.transfer: Create two benchmark protocols: one for interactive p95 latency and one for sustained batch throughput. Explain why their collection windows, summaries and conclusions differ.

lessons.title: SIMD, cache blocking, NUMA and job scheduling
lessons.outcome: Optimize locality and parallelism together.
lessons.practical_assignment: Optimize a particle or transform workload using one locality change and one scheduling change. Pass: test tail sizes, report numerical differences, and measure small as well as large workloads to expose overhead.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: parallel memory patterns; R48: multiprocessors and memory systems; R11: safe C++ and concurrency.
original_quiz: What is false sharing?
Why can very small jobs be inefficient?
Why test small workloads after a parallel optimization?
lessons.body:
### Locality and parallelism share a budget
